subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the circle which passes through the origin and intersects the circles x² + y² − 4x + 6y + 10 = 0 and x² + y² + 12y + 6 = 0 orthogonally.

insider_note: Passing through the origin makes c = 0 immediately — use that fact to simplify BOTH orthogonality equations from the start, rather than carrying c through the algebra and setting it to 0 only at the end.

steps.label: Set up the circle and use the origin
steps.margin_note: First mark. c = 0 is the whole reason to use the origin — it removes one unknown at once.
lines: S = 0 passes through the origin O(0, 0)
steps.why: A circle through the origin must satisfy its own equation at (0, 0), and every term except c vanishes there — so c = 0 follows immediately, before any orthogonality condition is used.
common_mistakes: Substituting (0, 0) but forgetting that x² and y² also vanish, leaving a needless extra term.
Leaving c as an unknown and only discovering c = 0 much later by accident.
steps.memory_tip: Through the origin always means c = 0 for a circle — the fastest fact in the whole chapter.

steps.label: Apply the first orthogonal condition
steps.margin_note: Second mark. g′ = −2, f′ = 3, c′ = 10 come straight from the first given circle.
lines: S is orthogonal to x² + y² − 4x + 6y + 10 = 0
steps.why: Two circles cut orthogonally exactly when 2gg′ + 2ff′ = c + c′ — applying this standard test to the first given circle is one linear equation in g and f.
common_mistakes: Reading g′ and f′ with the wrong sign from −4x + 6y (they are −2 and 3, half the coefficients, not −4 and 6).
Forgetting the +10 on the right side that comes from c′.
steps.memory_tip: Orthogonal condition is always 2gg′ + 2ff′ = c + c′ — half of every coefficient, matched on both circles.

steps.label: Apply the second orthogonal condition
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The second circle has g″ = 0, which makes this equation solve for f directly.
lines: S is orthogonal to x² + y² + 12y + 6 = 0
steps.why: Applying the orthogonality test to the second circle gives a second equation; because that circle has no x term, this equation solves for f immediately.
common_mistakes: Missing that g″ = 0 (no x term in the second circle), and keeping a needless g term in this equation.
Solving for g instead of f from this equation.
steps.memory_tip: A circle with no x term has g″ = 0 — its orthogonality condition always isolates f on its own.

steps.label: Write the final circle
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark, for substituting g, f, c back into the general circle.
steps.why: With f, and then g, and c already known, substituting all three back into x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 gives the one specific circle satisfying every condition.
common_mistakes: Substituting g instead of 2g into the equation, which needs the coefficient 2g directly.
Leaving the equation with a fraction (−7/2)x instead of clearing it by multiplying through by 2.
steps.memory_tip: Always substitute 2g and 2f, not g and f, since those are the actual coefficients of x and y in the circle's equation.
